transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Alex Johnson (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Maya Lee (CTO, Alcyon), Daniel Park (ML Eng), Sam Ortiz (Product)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, i'm alex with redwood inference, joined by priya from our se team. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Maya (Alcyon): doing well, thanks. excited to see the hosted api demo - we're evaluating for chat features in our product.
[00:12] Daniel (Alcyon): yeah quick context: we currently run an internal model stack on prem, but latency spikes under load. main asks are low latency for chat, predictable costs, and tight control over PII.
[00:20] Alex: perfect, that's exactly what we'll cover, we'll walk the hosted api for chat and text gen basics, demo streaming, parameters, retries and then show the console and some optimize suggestions. priya will handle the deeper technical bits.
[00:30] Priya (Redwood SE): quick note — i'll show a live call using our sdk and also the console's per-route metrics, so you'll see latency numbers and token breakdowns.

[00:45] Alex: okay start with big picture: hosted api gives you a simple rest/ sdk interface for text generation and chat, we have curated models, streaming for low-latency token-by-token, function calling and structured outputs, and we expose parameters like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, also retry behavior and idempotency keys.
[01:10] Maya: couple quick qual questions — data residency? and key management?
[01:14] Priya: yes for hosted we have region controls, you can pin requests to regions, and for customer keys we integrate with customer-managed KMS for enterprise plans, plus SOC2 and audit logs. we'll share the security pack after.
[01:28] Daniel: good. what about token billing granularity? we need to compare per-token costs vs our infra.
[01:34] Alex: billing is per-token for generation, per-embedding for embeddings, console shows token breakdown per-route and per-token cost so you can attribute to features. we'll send an example bill.

[02:00] -- Demo start --
[02:05] Priya: i'm going to share my screen, i'll run a simple chat example using node sdk. code snippet: 
  - const response = await redwood.chat.create({ model: 'rw-chat-medium', messages, stream: true, temperature: 0.2, top_p: 0.9, max_tokens: 256 });
[02:28] Priya: note stream:true returns an event stream, we show tokens as they arrive so perceived latency is lowest. (transcription artifact: sometimes 'stream' is written as 'scream' by auto gen)
[02:40] Daniel: how do you handle partial failures when streaming? if a connection drops mid-response?
[02:44] Priya: good q. we recommend idempotency keys for create calls and a retry strategy on the client. server side we support resumable streams in certain model variants (not all), and the SDK provides helpers for reconnect and resume. if resume not available, the client should retry the request with same idempotency key and the server will dedupe if possible.
[03:15] Alex: and to be explicit for retries, we advise exponential backoff with jitter, limit to a small number of retries for streaming to avoid duplicate tokens. also include a uniqueness id on user messages so downstream de-dupe is simpler.

[03:45] Priya: switching to params — temperature controls randomness, top_p controls nucleus sampling, max_tokens limits, stop sequences let you end an open generation. live demo changing temperature from 0.2 to 0.8 to show diversity.
[04:05] -- audio clip: demo showing different outputs --
[04:30] Daniel: how do you recommend we choose max_tokens for chat vs completions?
[04:34] Priya: for chat you typically set a generous max_tokens but enforce server-side and client-side truncation of long history. we also suggest prefix/KV caching for long-running conversations to avoid re-encoding the whole context on every call. caching reduces both latency and token usage.

[05:00] Maya: you mentioned kv cache, is that part of hosted? how does it work with multiple model variants?
[05:05] Priya: yes, hosted supports automatic kv caching for compatible models. the runtime stores recent kv segments and we can route to the same model variant to reuse the cache. if you route to a quantized or smaller variant we may need to rebuild cache, so routing policies are important — you can configure fallbacks in the console.

[05:40] Daniel: let's talk retries for non-streaming requests — i.e. batch completions — how are idempotency keys handled and what about exactly-once?
[05:50] Alex: idempotency keys are included as a header or param, server dedupes requests within a window; we don't guarantee global exactly-once for all models but dedupe window handles typical client retries. for critical flows you can store server-side state keyed by idempotency key.

[06:25] Priya: moving to rate limiting — hosted enforces per-account and per-route limits, SDK returns 429 with retry-after. best practice: implement client-side token bucket and exponential backoff with jitter, but also use our rate-limit headers to adapt. for heavy throughput we suggest dedicated capacity.

[07:00] -- Console demo --
[07:05] Priya: switching to the console, here is the routes page, you can see usage, latency P95, token cost breakdown and per-route throttles. you can create a route pinned to a model and set fallbacks, for example pinned to rw-chat-medium and fallback to rw-chat-small.
[07:30] Alex: the console's rollout feature lets you do canary percentages across model versions, and you can automatically fall back on latency SLO violations. we've seen customers reduce downtime by 30% with automatic fallbacks.

[08:05] Maya: curious about observability: can we get traces per request and token-level cost?
[08:10] Priya: yes, console exposes traces, token breakdown and you can hook our tracing headers into your APM. there's also raw logs in the audit trail for enterprise.

[08:40] Daniel: ok, what about caching in Optimize — you mentioned batching and quantization earlier?
[08:46] Priya: right, Optimize automations analyze your workload and suggest batching windows, cache strategies (prefix vs kv) and quantization profiles by model. for instance if your workload is short turn chat with low latency, Optimize might suggest small batch sizes and KV caching; for background summarization jobs, it would suggest larger batches and int8 quantization to save cost.

[09:20] Alex: an example: for high-throughput chat, batching 8-16 requests with dynamic padding and prefix cache can cut token cost ~20-40% while keeping P95 in target. we'll share a guideline doc.

[09:45] -- Questions on security/compliance --
[09:48] Maya: send over SOC2 and encryption docs, and how sso/ s a m l works with console. also need to understand retention policies for logs and transcripts.
[09:58] Alex: we'll include our SOC2 report, SAML SSO guide, and options for log retention/archival. retention can be configured and enterprise contracts include options for short retention or no retention for sensitive flows.

[10:15] Daniel: what about private keys, HSM? we have strict key policies.
[10:18] Priya: enterprise plans can integrate with customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and HSM via partner setups for private deployments. for hosted, we can allow envelope encryption with customer KMS so Redwood does not have cleartext keys.

[10:45] -- Back to technical: streaming reliability and reconnect patterns --
[10:50] Priya: some models support resumable streams via a resume token, most of the time clients implement reconnect and dedupe by idempotency. the sdk provides helpers but depending on your network patterns you might want sticky sessions or websocket reconnect logic.

[11:20] Maya: is streaming over websocket or server-sent events?
[11:23] Priya: both supported; node sdk defaults to event stream over http/2 or SSE; websockets are available for persist connections. SSE is simple for browser clients.

[11:40] Daniel: any gotchas with browser-based streaming?
[11:43] Priya: CORS and connection limits, also keep-alive times, we recommend using short-lived signing tokens from your backend so you don't expose the main API key in client-side.

[12:05] Alex: let's cover model selection briefly: you can pick a model optimized for latency, one for quality, or quantized variants for cost. Redwood's model catalog shows verified perf profiles with P50/P95 and cost estimates.

[12:30] Daniel: how do we benchmark? what artifacts should we provide for you to run a fair test?
[12:35] Priya: ideal: provide sample prompt set, typical user concurrency, expected tokens per request, and SLA targets. we'll run a benchmark with our harness and share raw numbers and recommendations — we'll test streaming latency, end-to-end percieved latency, and throughput.

[13:05] Sam (Product): curious about developer ergonomics — sdks and examples for ruby/python/go?
[13:09] Alex: we have official sdks for js/python/go/ruby, plus curl examples and open-source quickstarts. code samples are in the repo and we'll share a quickstart link.

[13:30] -- Demo of error handling --
[13:35] Priya: intentionally cause a 429 by exceeding a small token bucket, sdk shows 429 with retry-after. demo implement backoff: set initial delay 200ms, multiply by 2 with jitter. also show how to use idempotency key header: x-idempotency-key.

[14:10] Daniel: suppose a partial token wrote to user, but then retry causes duplication and user sees repeated words — any server dedupe for token level?
[14:18] Priya: the server can't know what user already displayed; that's client-side de-duplication territory. best practice: include sequence ids on incremental tokens and client drop duplicates. for critical flows, include final message confirmation on server with idempotency.

[14:45] Maya: what's the SLA for hosted?
[14:48] Alex: standard hosted has a best-effort SLA, enterprise/dedicated plans include SLA-backed latency and uptime commitments. we'll include SLA terms in the contract pack.

[15:05] -- Optimize recommendations example --
[15:10] Priya: show optimize dashboard: it surfaces hot prompts, high-cost routes, and suggests quantization for large-batch offline jobs, or suggests per-route batching for similar short prompts. you can auto-apply recommendations as experiments and measure regression via eval sets.

[15:40] Daniel: evals — does Redwood support automated eval suites?
[15:44] Priya: yes, you can upload prompt sets and expected outputs, Redwood runs continuous evals on model rollouts and alerts on regressions. it's integrated with the console.

[16:10] Maya: any notable limitations for multi-tenant data separation on hosted? we have strict compliance needs.

[16:18] Alex: hosted has logical separation and strong access controls, but for strict isolation we recommend Dedicated or Private which give physical or network separation and optional private control plane.

[16:35] Daniel: we might start hosted for quick POC and move to dedicated. how painful is migration?
[16:40] Priya: designed to be smooth — same api and config surface across hosted/dedicated/private. you'll pin model versions, routing policies can be moved, and console configs export/import. migration testing is recommended but we help with runbooks.

[17:05] -- Closing demo bits, quick Q&A --
[17:10] Alex: recap — streaming gives token-by-token low perceived latency, param tuning controls randomness and length, use idempotency keys + backoff for retries, use console and optimize to tune batching and caching. next steps are the POC and security docs.

[17:28] Maya: sounds good. can you include expected costs for a 100k monthly chat calls baseline?
[17:32] Alex: yes we'll provide an example cost model and per-token estimates.

[17:45] Sam: send links to sdks and quickstarts.

[17:48] Alex: will do.

[18:00] -- small crosstalk and wrap up --
[18:05] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll get the sample traffic and you can send keys.

[18:08] Alex: great thanks, priya and i will follow up with starter pack, security docs and schedule the se deep dive for next week.

[18:15] Daniel: thanks all.

[18:30] -- end meeting --
